definition: The looped background music a land plays to set its mood, usually without lyrics so it never competes with speech.
Sound from one themed zone leaking into a neighbouring zone where it breaks the theme.
A small speaker placed low and close to guests so sound stays local instead of carrying across a land.
A long, seamless recording of environmental sound such as birds, wind or distant machinery that plays continuously in a space.
Disney's nickname for a fan-driven scent dispenser that pushes a chosen aroma into a scene or street on a schedule.
A replaceable cartridge soaked with fragrance that a scent machine blows air across to release the smell.
A Kelvin number describing how warm (orange) or cool (blue) a white light looks; candlelight is low, overcast sky is high.
A row of small colour thumbnails showing how colour and light change beat by beat through a story or ride.
A family of muted grey-greens Disney paints on fences, show buildings and utilities so the eye slides past them.
Paint and texture applied to a cheap or durable base to make it read as another material, such as aged wood or stone.
A thin, dark, translucent coat of paint that settles into recesses to make a new surface look old and dirty.
Everything underfoot: paving colour, pattern, texture and scoring, treated as a designed storytelling surface.
The local weather of a small space, shaped by shade, wind, water and surfaces, which can differ from the regional forecast.
The combined heat a person feels from surrounding surfaces and sun; shade lowers it even when air temperature does not change.
A temporary re-dressing of an attraction or land for a holiday, installed and removed on a yearly cycle.
The idea that people prefer places where they can see out (prospect) while feeling sheltered (refuge).
Our innate pull toward living things and natural settings, which planting and water in parks quietly satisfy.
Bitner's term for the built environment of a service, covering ambient conditions, layout and signs, and how it shapes behaviour.
Kotler's term for deliberately designing the sensory qualities of a space to produce a wanted response in visitors.
Density is people per area; crowding is the unpleasant feeling that there are too many of them, which design can change.
Edward Hall's study of the distances people keep from each other and how space shapes those distances.
How easily a scene reads as one organised whole; high coherence lets rich detail feel calm instead of noisy.
Kaplan's theory that softly fascinating natural scenes let the tired, effortful kind of attention recover.
Deliberately choosing surfaces guests will touch so texture and temperature support the story and survive wear.
